q: 4.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. What is its molarity?
x: Moles of NaOH = 4.0/40 = 0.10 mol; volume = 0.250 dm³; molarity = 0.10/0.250 = 0.40 mol dm⁻³. Stopping at 0.10 forgets the volume; multiplying by 0.250 gives 0.025; dividing grams by volume gives 16.

q: 9.0 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹), is dissolved in 250 g of water. What is the molality of the solution?
x: Moles of glucose = 9.0/180 = 0.050 mol; mass of solvent = 0.250 kg; molality = 0.050/0.250 = 0.20 mol kg⁻¹. Forgetting to divide by the solvent mass gives 0.050; dividing grams of solute by grams of water gives 0.036.

q: 46 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is mixed with 36 g of water. What is the mole fraction of ethanol in the mixture?
x: Ethanol = 46/46 = 1.0 mol; water = 36/18 = 2.0 mol; mole fraction of ethanol = 1.0/(1.0 + 2.0) = 0.33. Using masses (46/82) gives 0.56, the mass fraction; 0.67 is the mole fraction of water.

q: A 500 g sample of water contains 0.0020 g of dissolved lead. What is the concentration of lead in parts per million by mass?
x: ppm = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 10⁶ = (0.0020/500) × 10⁶ = 4.0 ppm. Slipping a power of ten in 10⁶ gives 0.40 or 40 ppm.

q: Concentrated sulphuric acid is 98% H₂SO₄ by mass and has a density of 1.84 g cm⁻³. What is its molarity?
x: 1 dm³ has mass 1000 × 1.84 = 1840 g, of which 98% = 1803.2 g is H₂SO₄ = 1803.2/98 = 18.4 mol, so 18.4 mol dm⁻³. Ignoring the density (taking 1000 g) gives 10.0; counting two H⁺ per molecule gives 36.8.

q: What volume of water must be added to 100 cm³ of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution to dilute it to 0.20 mol dm⁻³?
x: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂: 0.50 × 100 = 0.20 × V₂, so V₂ = 250 cm³ final volume; water to add = 250 − 100 = 150 cm³. Giving the final volume (250 cm³) instead of the water added is the commonest slip; 40 cm³ comes from inverting the ratio.

q: Molality is often preferred to molarity when colligative properties are measured over a range of temperatures because molality:
o: Depends only on masses, which do not change with temperature, whereas the volume of a solution does
Is always numerically larger than molarity
Takes into account the dissociation of electrolytes
Depends on the volume of the solvent, which stays constant
x: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so it uses masses only; molarity uses the volume of solution, which expands or contracts with temperature. Molality does not depend on volume at all, and it says nothing about dissociation.

q: An aqueous solution of a solute of molar mass 50 g mol⁻¹ has a concentration of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ and a density of 1.10 g cm⁻³. What is its molality?
x: 1 dm³ of solution has mass 1100 g and contains 2.0 × 50 = 100 g of solute, so the water is 1000 g = 1.000 kg; molality = 2.0/1.000 = 2.0 mol kg⁻¹. Dividing by the mass of the whole solution (1.10 kg) gives 1.8; multiplying by the density gives 2.2.

q: 250 cm³ of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution is mixed with 750 cm³ of 0.40 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution. What is the molarity of NaCl in the mixture?
x: Moles = 0.250 × 0.20 + 0.750 × 0.40 = 0.050 + 0.30 = 0.35 mol in 1.00 dm³, so 0.35 mol dm⁻³. Averaging the two concentrations without weighting by volume gives 0.30; adding them gives 0.60.

q: Liquids X and Y form an ideal solution. At 300 K the vapour pressures of pure X and pure Y are 100 kPa and 40 kPa. What is the vapour pressure of a solution in which the mole fraction of X is 0.25?
x: By Raoult's law, p = x(X)p°(X) + x(Y)p°(Y) = 0.25 × 100 + 0.75 × 40 = 25 + 30 = 55 kPa. Swapping the mole fractions gives 0.75 × 100 + 0.25 × 40 = 85 kPa; a plain average gives 70 kPa.

q: An ideal liquid mixture of X (pure vapour pressure 100 kPa) and Y (pure vapour pressure 40 kPa) has mole fraction of X = 0.25. What is the mole fraction of X in the vapour in equilibrium with it?
x: Partial pressures: p(X) = 0.25 × 100 = 25 kPa and p(Y) = 0.75 × 40 = 30 kPa, total 55 kPa. By Dalton's law, the mole fraction of X in the vapour = 25/55 ≈ 0.45, richer in the more volatile X than the liquid. Assuming the vapour has the same composition as the liquid gives 0.25; 0.55 is the mole fraction of Y in the vapour.

q: Which description fits an ideal solution?
o: It obeys Raoult's law only when very dilute, and heat is given out on mixing
Its vapour pressure is always higher than Raoult's law predicts
Its two components have equal vapour pressures when pure
It obeys Raoult's law at all compositions, with no heat change and no volume change on mixing
x: In an ideal solution the attractions between unlike molecules equal those between like molecules, so ΔH(mixing) = 0, ΔV(mixing) = 0 and Raoult's law holds at every composition. A vapour pressure above Raoult's prediction is a positive deviation, a feature of non-ideal solutions.

q: Which pair of liquids forms a nearly ideal solution?
x: Benzene and toluene have very similar non-polar molecules and intermolecular forces, so their mixture follows Raoult's law closely. Ethanol and water show positive deviation, while acetone with chloroform and nitric acid with water show negative deviation, because their unlike-molecule attractions differ from those in the pure liquids.

q: A mixture of chloroform, CHCl₃, and acetone, CH₃COCH₃, has a lower vapour pressure than Raoult's law predicts. The reason is that:
o: Attractions in the mixture are weaker than in the pure liquids
Hydrogen bonds form between the H of CHCl₃ and the O of acetone, so attractions in the mixture are stronger than in the pure liquids
The two liquids react completely to form a new compound
Chloroform molecules are much heavier than acetone molecules
x: The C–H of chloroform is made polar by three Cl atoms and hydrogen-bonds to the carbonyl oxygen of acetone; molecules escape less easily, giving a negative deviation (and heat is given out on mixing). Weaker attractions would raise the vapour pressure, a positive deviation.

q: A pair of liquids shows a large positive deviation from Raoult's law and forms an azeotrope. This azeotropic mixture:
o: Boils at a higher temperature than either pure liquid
Boils at a lower temperature than either pure liquid
Boils at a temperature between the boiling points of the two pure liquids
Can be separated into its pure components by fractional distillation
x: A large positive deviation gives a maximum in vapour pressure, so the azeotrope boils at a minimum temperature, lower than both components, and distils unchanged in composition. A maximum-boiling azeotrope comes from negative deviation, the usual mix-up.

q: 0.10 mol of a non-volatile solute is dissolved in 0.90 mol of water at a temperature where pure water has a vapour pressure of 3.0 kPa. Assuming Raoult's law, what is the vapour pressure of the solution?
x: Only water contributes vapour: p = x(water) × p°(water) = (0.90/1.00) × 3.0 = 2.7 kPa. Using the solute's mole fraction gives 0.30 kPa, which is actually the lowering of vapour pressure; a solute never raises the solvent's vapour pressure.

q: In a solution of liquids P and Q, the P–Q attractions are weaker than the P–P and Q–Q attractions. Compared with an ideal solution, the vapour pressure, heat change and volume change on mixing are:
o: Lower vapour pressure; heat given out; volume decreases
Higher vapour pressure; heat given out; volume decreases
Higher vapour pressure; heat absorbed; volume increases
Lower vapour pressure; heat absorbed; volume increases
x: Weaker unlike attractions let molecules escape more easily (positive deviation, higher vapour pressure); energy is needed to separate like molecules that is not repaid, so mixing absorbs heat (ΔH > 0); the molecules sit farther apart, so the volume increases (ΔV > 0). The second option describes negative deviation.

q: Liquids P and Q form an ideal solution. At one temperature, a solution with mole fraction of P = 0.50 has a vapour pressure of 60 kPa, and one with mole fraction of P = 0.25 has 50 kPa. What is the vapour pressure of pure P?
x: 0.50p°(P) + 0.50p°(Q) = 60 gives p°(P) + p°(Q) = 120; 0.25p°(P) + 0.75p°(Q) = 50 gives p°(P) + 3p°(Q) = 200. Subtracting, 2p°(Q) = 80, so p°(Q) = 40 kPa and p°(P) = 80 kPa. Check: 0.25 × 80 + 0.75 × 40 = 50. 40 kPa is pure Q, the tempting mix-up.

q: Colligative properties of a dilute solution depend on:
o: The chemical nature of the solute
The colour of the solute particles
The number of solute particles in a given amount of solvent, not their nature
The shape of the solute molecules
x: Vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on how many solute particles are present per amount of solvent. That is why 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ glucose and 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ urea give the same freezing-point depression although they are different substances.

q: 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water. Kb of water = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹. At what temperature does the solution boil at 1 atm?
x: Moles = 18/180 = 0.10 mol in 0.500 kg, so molality = 0.20 mol kg⁻¹ and ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.20 = 0.104 K; the boiling point is 100.104 °C. Taking 0.10 mol as the molality (forgetting the 0.500 kg) gives 100.052 °C; subtracting gives 99.896 °C, a freezing-type mistake.

q: 2.0 g of a non-volatile non-electrolyte dissolved in 50 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 1.0 K. Kf of benzene = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹. What is the molar mass of the solute?
x: Molality = ΔTf/Kf = 1.0/5.12 mol kg⁻¹; moles in 0.050 kg = 0.050/5.12; molar mass = 2.0 ÷ (0.050/5.12) = 2.0 × 5.12/0.050 = 204.8 ≈ 205 g mol⁻¹. Using 100 g of benzene by mistake gives 102; leaving out the solvent mass altogether gives 10.2.

q: Which 0.10 mol kg⁻¹ aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? (Assume the salts are fully dissociated.)
x: Freezing-point depression depends on the number of particles: CaCl₂ gives 3 ions (0.30 mol kg⁻¹ of particles), NaCl gives 2, and glucose and urea stay as single molecules. The most particles give the biggest depression and so the lowest freezing point. Treating every solute as one particle makes them all look the same.

q: What is the osmotic pressure of a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution at 27 °C? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: π = CRT = 0.10 × 0.0821 × 300 = 2.46 atm, with T = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Using 27 instead of 300 gives 0.22 atm, the forgot-to-convert-to-kelvin slip; dropping the 0.10 gives 24.6 atm.

q: Dissolving a non-volatile solute in water raises the boiling point because the solute:
o: Lowers the vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed for it to reach the external pressure
Raises the vapour pressure of the water
Increases the external pressure on the liquid
Forms covalent bonds with the water molecules
x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Solute particles lower the vapour pressure of the solvent, so the solution must be heated above the normal boiling point to reach that pressure. A higher vapour pressure would lower the boiling point, the reverse of what happens.

q: Which solution is isotonic with (has the same osmotic pressure as) 0.30 mol dm⁻³ glucose solution at the same temperature? (Assume the salts are fully dissociated.)
x: Osmotic pressure depends on total particle concentration: glucose gives 0.30 mol dm⁻³ of particles; 0.15 NaCl gives 2 × 0.15 = 0.30. 0.30 NaCl gives 0.60, 0.60 urea gives 0.60, and 0.30 CaCl₂ gives 0.90. Forgetting that NaCl splits into two ions makes 0.30 NaCl look right.

q: 3.0 g of a non-electrolyte is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. At 300 K its osmotic pressure is 0.821 atm. What is the molar mass of the solute? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: C = π/RT = 0.821/(0.0821 × 300) = 1/30 mol dm⁻³; moles in 0.250 dm³ = 0.250/30 = 1/120 mol; molar mass = 3.0 × 120 = 360 g mol⁻¹. Treating 3.0 g as if it were in 1 dm³ gives 90 (the 250 cm³ forgotten).

q: Equal masses of urea (molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹) and glucose (molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹) are dissolved in separate, equal masses of water. What is the ratio of the freezing-point depression of the urea solution to that of the glucose solution?
x: For equal masses, moles are inversely proportional to molar mass: urea gives 180/60 = 3 times as many moles as glucose, so its molality and ΔTf are 3 times larger. Reasoning that a heavier molecule has a bigger effect gives 1 : 3; equal masses do not mean equal particles, so 1 : 1 is wrong.

q: An aqueous solution of sodium carbonate turns red litmus blue because:
o: Na⁺ ions react with water to form NaOH and H⁺ ions
Sodium carbonate crystals contain OH⁻ ions
CO₃²⁻ ions react with water to form HCO₃⁻ and OH⁻ ions
CO₃²⁻ ions take OH⁻ from water, leaving H⁺ ions
x: Carbonate is the anion of the weak acid H₂CO₃, so it hydrolyses: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻, giving excess OH⁻. Na⁺ comes from the strong base NaOH and does not hydrolyse; if CO₃²⁻ removed OH⁻, the solution would be acidic, not basic.

q: Which 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous salt solution has the highest pH?
x: CH₃COONa is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base; CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyses to give OH⁻, so the pH is above 7. NaCl (strong acid, strong base) is neutral, while NH₄Cl and AlCl₃ (cations of a weak base) hydrolyse to give H⁺ and are acidic. Thinking any sodium salt is neutral gives NaCl.

q: Which ion has the most exothermic hydration enthalpy?
x: Hydration enthalpy grows with charge density: a smaller ion with a higher charge attracts the polar water molecules more strongly. Al³⁺ is the smallest and most highly charged of these, so it releases the most energy; K⁺, the largest with the lowest charge, releases the least. Looking only at size or only at charge can mislead.

q: Anhydrous CuSO₄ gives out heat when it dissolves in water, but CuSO₄·5H₂O absorbs heat when it dissolves. The best explanation is that:
o: The pentahydrate has no lattice energy to overcome
In the anhydrous salt the Cu²⁺ ions release a large hydration energy on dissolving, while in the pentahydrate they are already largely hydrated
The anhydrous salt reacts with water, but the pentahydrate does not dissolve at all
The pentahydrate contains more ions per formula unit
x: The heat of solution balances lattice breaking against hydration. Bare Cu²⁺ ions of the anhydrous salt are hydrated strongly as they dissolve, and this outweighs the lattice energy. In CuSO₄·5H₂O the Cu²⁺ already holds water, so little hydration energy is left and lattice breaking dominates. Every crystal has a lattice energy, and both salts dissolve.

q: The particles of the dispersed phase in a colloid have diameters roughly in the range:
x: Colloidal particles lie between those of a true solution (below about 1 nm) and a suspension (above about 1000 nm, i.e. 10⁻⁶ m). Particles of 0.1 mm or more are visible and settle out as a suspension; below 0.1 nm is smaller than an atom.

q: Which observation can tell a colloidal solution apart from a true solution?
o: Passing it through ordinary filter paper
Whether it looks clear to the eye
The Tyndall effect, the visible path of a light beam through the liquid
x: Colloidal particles are large enough to scatter light, so a beam shows a visible path; particles in a true solution are too small to do this. Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper, and many colloids look clear and coloured, so filtration and appearance cannot tell them apart.

q: Brownian movement of colloidal particles is caused by:
o: Uneven bombardment of the particles by molecules of the dispersion medium
Attraction between the electric charges on the particles
x: Molecules of the medium strike each colloidal particle from all sides, but not equally at every instant, so the particle is pushed in a random zigzag path. Particles of the same sol carry like charges, which repel, and gravity would cause settling rather than random motion.

q: Which substance forms a lyophilic (solvent-loving) colloid when mixed with water?
x: Starch molecules interact strongly with water and form a stable sol directly on warming, which can be re-formed after drying: a lyophilic colloid. Sols of gold, As₂S₃ and Fe(OH)₃ have little attraction for water, must be made by special methods and are easily coagulated by electrolytes: they are lyophobic.
